Describe the SIFT detector: scale-space construction, extrema detection, and keypoint filtering.
risposta: SIFT finds keypoints as extrema in scale-space. It builds a Gaussian pyramid in octaves (same-resolution images progressively blurred; subsample by 2 to start the next octave, doubling scale) and forms a Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) pyramid, DoG=G(x,y,k*sigma)-G(x,y,sigma), as an efficient approximation of the LoG blob detector. A candidate keypoint is a pixel that is a local max/min versus its 8 spatial neighbors plus 9 in the level above and 9 below (26 total). Low-contrast keypoints (low DoG) are discarded as unstable, and edge responses are rejected because along an edge the DoG changes strongly in only one direction and is not distinct enough for matching.

domanda: Explain SIFT orientation assignment and the construction of the 128-dim descriptor, and list the descriptor's invariances.
risposta: Orientation assignment makes the descriptor rotation-invariant: in a neighborhood around the keypoint (in its Gaussian image) compute gradient magnitude/orientation, build a 36-bin orientation histogram with votes weighted by magnitude and a Gaussian window; the highest peak is the canonical orientation, and any peak above 80% of it creates an additional keypoint. The descriptor: take a 16x16 window at the characteristic scale, rotate coordinates/gradients by the canonical orientation, divide into a 4x4 grid of cells, compute an 8-bin orientation histogram per cell, concatenate into a 128-dim vector, and normalize to unit length. SIFT is invariant to scale (scale-space detection), rotation (orientation normalization), and illumination (vector normalization), and robust to affine transforms and noise.

domanda: Explain feature matching with Lowe's ratio test and the metrics used to evaluate matching performance.
risposta: To match a source keypoint to a target image, the naive approach takes the nearest neighbor by Euclidean distance, but this yields many false matches for ambiguous features. Lowe's ratio test instead finds the two nearest neighbors f2 and f2' and accepts the match only if ||f1-f2||/||f1-f2'|| is below a threshold (e.g. 0.75-0.8), rejecting ambiguous matches. Evaluation uses ground truth: varying a threshold gives an ROC curve of True Positive Rate (recall) vs False Positive Rate, summarized by AUC (1.0 perfect, 0.5 random). Plain accuracy is misleading because true negatives dominate; precision (TP/(TP+FP)), recall (TP/(TP+FN)), and their harmonic mean F1 are more informative.

domanda: Compare SURF and binary descriptors (ORB) with SIFT in terms of how they achieve speed.
risposta: SURF is a faster SIFT alternative: it detects blobs where det(H) of the Hessian is maximal, approximates the Gaussian second derivatives with box filters computed instantly via integral images (det approx = Dxx*Dyy-(w*Dxy)^2, w~0.9), assigns orientation via Haar wavelet responses, and builds a 64-dim descriptor from sums of Haar responses over a 4x4 grid. Binary descriptors are even cheaper: they encode each bit by a simple intensity comparison between a pixel pair, producing a short bit string (e.g. 256 bits) compared by fast Hamming distance. ORB improves BRIEF by adding rotation invariance (rotating learned sampling pairs around the patch center of mass) and learning 256 uncorrelated, high-variance pairs for discriminativeness.
